speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This three-in-one feature is unique to our CPF system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We regularly review and update the CPF system and the Bill brings into legal effect the following changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This Bill will give effect to this by ceasing non-residents' participation in CPF schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Second, the Bill introduces amendments to clarify and streamline the administration of CPF schemes for better service delivery to residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The first set of amendments brings us closer to the CPF system's core objective of helping residents meet their retirement, housing and healthcare needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: As non-residents may choose to leave Singapore permanently at any point in time and are not expected to reside in Singapore in the long term, they are responsible for their own retirement and healthcare adequacy or home-ownership needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have gradually reduced the participation of non-residents in CPF schemes over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Non-residents have not been required to make CPF contributions since 1995.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The option to make voluntary contributions was also removed in 2003.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, those who already had CPF accounts have been allowed to leave their past contributions in their accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The amendments to completely cease the participation of non-residents in CPF schemes are the final steps that put the CPF system's core focus on supporting residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: CPF savings that are not transferred by this date will be transferred to the General Moneys of the Fund and will no longer earn the prevailing CPF interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is because non-residents can transfer their monies to their bank account at any time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: From 1 April 2027, three years after the change kicks in, non-residents' monies in the General Moneys of the Fund will no longer earn any interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Non-residents are, therefore, encouraged to transfer these monies to their own bank accounts as soon as they can.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Non-residents' participation in CPF schemes, such as CPF LIFE, will also cease from 1 April 2024.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: With these changes, the resources dedicated for the administration of CPF schemes will be better focused on supporting the needs of residents who have a long-term commitment to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The second set of amendments clarifies as well as streamlines the administration of CPF schemes so as to improve service delivery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, under the CPF Act, members need to explicitly authorise CPF Board to allow any person to access their CPF information after their demise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For those who were authorised by the deceased member, they still have to write in to CPF Board to obtain the deceased member's information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For those who are not authorised by the deceased to access the deceased member's CPF information, they would have to take the additional step of obtaining a Court order to access the information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Such processes complicate the handling of a deceased member's CPF account and add additional stress to families in bereavement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will amend the CPF Act to make post-demise handling more convenient for the nominees and beneficiaries under the relevant intestacy laws of CPF members who have passed away.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The amendments will allow nominees and beneficiaries under the relevant intestacy laws to access CPF information of deceased members, without members needing to explicitly authorise CPF Board to do so before they pass on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The CPF information that will be disclosed includes details, such as the deceased members' CPF balances, names of all the nominees and the proportion of CPF monies that the nominees will receive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: It will also include details of the CPF schemes which the deceased members had participated in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is aligned to industry practices for wills and intestate distribution of assets by the Public Trustee where, generally, all beneficiaries are able to obtain information on the portion of the estate or assets each beneficiary will have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Being able to access the deceased members' CPF information will also provide transparency to the nominees and beneficiaries under the relevant intestacy laws that the deceased members' CPF monies have been fully accounted for and disbursed accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The amendments will also clarify that CPF Board can process CPF transactions on or after a member's death.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, under the CPF Act, CPF Board should, generally, process CPF-related transactions up to the date of death of a member.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The amendments will make clear that CPF Board is empowered to process certain transactions on or after the date of death of the member.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These transactions typically arise or follow from obligations preceding the death of the member.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: They include inflows to the CPF accounts, such as refund of CareShield Life premiums to the member's MediSave account after death; and outflows from the CPF accounts, such as refunds to employers, if there were excess CPF contributions made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, the Act requires CPF Board to prescribe the form of the Notice to Attend Court in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: With the amendments, CPF Board can make changes to the notice without having to amend subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is aligned with legislation governing other public sector agencies and allows for greater ease of administration when changes to the notice are required.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: CPF Board will publish a sample copy of the Notice to Attend Court on CPF Board's website so that members of the public can easily access and verify the authenticity and legitimacy of any notice received.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This means greater convenience for CPF members, employers and other persons as they will be able to access more documents from CPF Board electronically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For a start, selected hardcopy documents, notifications, such as the Notice of Contributions issued by CPF Board to self-employed persons, will be served electronically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Self-employed persons will still have the option to receive a hardcopy notice, by simply going to the CPF website to indicate their preference.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: It also clarifies and streamlines the administration of CPF schemes, such as by aligning with industry practices, to benefit residents and provide them with greater convenience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many such accounts will be affected and what percentage of all CPF accounts do they constitute?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there any particular demographic of workers that is especially affected by this change?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As these workers will be entitled to withdraw all existing monies once they lose their right to participate in the CPF scheme, are we doing anything special to brace ourselves for the expected rate of outflow of monies from the system?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it is understandable that we want to ring-fence the benefits of the CPF system to Singaporeans only, I am sure there were also good reasons why we allowed foreigners working here to participate in the CPF scheme previously.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Government share how those considerations have changed today?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One reason that immediately comes to my mind is to ensure the relative competitiveness and employability of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By disapplying the CPF system to foreigners working here, would that cause businesses and employers to turn away from Singaporeans to foreign workers since they do not have to pay additional CPF contributions for the foreign workers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the CPF system becomes inapplicable to non-PR foreigners, related schemes, such as the Lifelong Income Scheme and the Home Protection Insurance Scheme, will naturally have to be terminated for such individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am just curious why the Bill expressly provides that the time prescribed for terminating such schemes "may differ for different classes of members".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps the Minister can provide some clarification on what the provision seeks to address.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is the move to ring-fence the benefits of CPF to Singaporeans a sign that we will be seeing significant changes to the system?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When many Members, including me, queried the relevance of the CPF interest rate pegs amidst soaring inflation and global interest rates, Minister Tan See Leng stated during the Committee of Supply 2023 that the Ministry is watching this interest rate environment very closely to ensure that the CPF interest rate pegs remain relevant in the prevailing operating environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are we about to see an increase in the 2.5% and 4% pegs for the CPF Ordinary Account (OA) and other accounts respectively?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad that we are taking steps to make it even easier for a CPF member's monies to be disbursed to beneficiaries upon the member's death.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When we last debated amendments to the CPF Act in 2021, this House was informed of how CPF Board already reaches out to nominees once it is notified of a member's death and it disburses the monies within a month.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill now introduces a power for the CPF Board to disclose certain information about the deceased CPF member to his or her nominees or any persons who would be the member's beneficiaries if no nomination was made.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would enable nominees and beneficiaries to come forward and withdraw the member's leftover CPF monies even more quickly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under the new section 59(11), the information which CPF Board may disclose without consent includes the deceased member's CPF accounts, any nomination made by the member and "any other information as may be prescribed in regulations".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the question I have is: will the prescribed information be broader than the scope of information that a member can presently consent to the CPF Board's disclosure?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the culmination of changes to CPF that began almost 30 years ago.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Prior to August 1995, some categories of foreign workers, most notably, Employment Pass (EP) holders, had to make CPF contributions in line with the prevailing rates of Singaporeans and PRs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similarly, their employers also had to make CPF contributions for these foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, after 1 August 1995, all foreigners were exempted from CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At that time, the Ministry of Labour, which is now the Ministry of Manpower, stated that the only reason for the change was to streamline the CPF rule for all foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But even in 1995, there was already concern that exempting foreign workers, especially EP holders, from CPF contributions would have negative impacts on Singaporean workers, especially the middle-ranking PMETs, because employers would benefit from lower wage cost when they employ new foreign staff.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An article in The Straits Times on 15 July 1995 noted that Singaporean workers would become less competitive against foreigners if employers do not make up for all or some of the CPF forgone by the foreign worker, especially if the foreigner was here on local terms.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even the then Menteri Besar of Johor, Mr Abdul Ghani bin Othman expressed his concern that the rule change would make Singapore a more attractive place to work for Malaysians, especially those from Johor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can now examine this with the benefit of the experience of the last 30 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the rule change in 1995, the number of EP holders in Singapore has increased substantially.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the mid-1990s, there were only 50,000 EP holders in Singapore, accounting for less than 3% of the labour force at that time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not suggesting that the exemption of EP holders from CPF contributions has been the only reason driving the increase in the number and proportion of EP holders among the workforce in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there is no doubt that this policy does make our local professionals less competitive against foreign professionals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As for the EP holder, the employer's wage bill remains as $5,000 and the EP holder gets to take home the whole $5,000.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a win-win situation for both the employer and the EP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should be no wonder that the employers in Singapore have become more reliant on EP holders since the rules were changed almost 30 years ago.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister for Manpower has denied that several times in this House in response to my questioning, quoting other costs that the employers have to bear.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the fact remains that the change of the law in 1995 has given an advantage to employers who employ foreign workers and PMETs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That advantage became a menace to Singaporean workers after the Government opened up the local job market to foreigners since the early 2000s.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are not calling for a return to the old days, where EP holders had to make CPF contributions, in line with Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we believe that, even until today, not enough has been done to mitigate the negative impacts caused by this policy, which has helped to make Singaporean workers less competitive against foreign workers and depress the wages of Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What can be done to mitigate these negative impacts?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP would like to put forth two suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have made this call in this House before, during the Budget debates in 2021 and 2023.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In March, the Minister said that I keep harping on this thing about imposing a levy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I am going to repeat this again.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This levy will take up a smaller portion of the high salaries of the true foreign talents and differentiate them from lower-wage foreign professionals who are being used as low-cost labour and depressing the wages of Singapore professionals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This way, we will be able to get the best, highest quality talent to come to Singapore from anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As CPF balances are long-term retirement funds kept with CPF Board for 30 to 40 years, there is room for the returns on CPF accounts to be higher.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans currently have limited options to increase the returns on their CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can only leave the money in their accounts and earn the fixed interest rates given by the Government, or invest savings above a threshold in the CPF Investment Scheme (CPFIS).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although the experience of the CPFIS, which is essentially a self-managed investment account is not encouraging, perhaps due to limited investor knowledge and lack of investment opportunities in the local capital markets, we should allow Singaporeans to put more of their CPF savings with professional managers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2016, the CPF Advisory Board had recommended that a new lifetime retirement investment scheme, which is managed by professionals, be introduced.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under this scheme, CPF members will be allowed to invest some of their CPF savings in simple-to-understand, low-fee, well-diversified life-cycle investment products.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such products will be passively managed and carefully selected by the CPF Board.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The funds would most likely invest in higher-risk, higher-return assets such as equities when the CPF member is younger and lower-risk, lower-return assets such as bonds when they are closer to their retirement age.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similar funds are offered by the Australian superannuation scheme or 401K scheme in America, which some Singaporeans may already be familiar with.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will be an additional option for most CPF members which may earn higher returns on their investable CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to statistics published by the US Department of Labor, 401K plans return about 6% to 10% per annum when we assess the rate of return over a five-year period.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the returns each year will be much more volatile than a fixed interest rate from CPF, CPF members should be able to earn a higher return through the lifetime retirement investment scheme over 30 or 40 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On top of this, the lifetime retirement investment scheme can help grow our local fund management industry and preventing Singaporeans from being over-invested in property.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is possible because GIC returns more than 4% a year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should share with Singaporeans more of the differential between what it pays Singaporeans in CPF interest and what it earns from GIC in investment returns.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will go a long way in improving the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans whose wages have been depressed by the influx of lower-wage foreign workers over the last few decades.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill also updates rules relating to the death of a CPF member.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CPF plays an important role in our social stability by helping Singaporeans have a strong retirement nest egg set aside to age gracefully.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support this Bill as it represents a continued focus on this purpose.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is how we ensure that new citizens or PRs will have sufficient amounts set aside for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The changes in this Bill reinforce that CPF is meant for the retirement needs of Singaporeans and PRs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are people who continue to take up citizenship or PR status.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the point that they take up citizenship or PR status, they may not have any CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Depending on their age, they may not have the time to build up their retirement reserves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If new citizens and PRs do not have sufficient retirement reserves, they too will have to rely on public infrastructure in their retirement years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How does the Government ensure that any new citizens and PRs have sufficient savings to be self-reliant in their retirement years?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the change of timing when making computations for deceased members.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate what practical effect these changes will have for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The CPF website states that there is no need for Singaporeans to notify the CPF Board.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Singaporeans assume that notifications are made automatically to the CPF Board on the same day a death is reported?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there any risk that this would adversely affect the accounts of a deceased member or payouts to their nominees?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CPF can appear complex to Singaporeans and making sure the rules are clear to Singaporeans will give them greater confidence in the system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final clarification is on the adjustment to CPF interest rates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are in an environment of rising interest rates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many Singaporeans save in and even voluntarily top up their CPF, knowing it is a safe vehicle for their retirement savings with an attractive interest rate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this year we saw the pegged rate for the Special and MediSave accounts go above the floor rate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Various savings and investment products are also advertising rates above the Ordinary Account interest rate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans may thus want to chase higher interest rates and through riskier products.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the Government's approach to adjusting the interest rate?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the rates be reviewed in the near future so that our ageing population can have a larger retirement nest egg?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, I seek clarification on the policy intent behind the closure of CPF accounts for non-SC/PR individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When was the requirement for CPF contributions by non-SC/PR members introduced?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Among them are those who received contributions or made voluntary contributions since 2003 as well as former SC/PRs who relinquished their citizenship or permanent residency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Were active steps taken to encourage SC/PRs to close their accounts over the years?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can CPF share projections regarding the number of individuals expected to transition to the Supplementary Retirement Scheme (SRS)?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Regarding the impact of individuals transitioning to the SRS, SRS contributions are entitled to income tax relief.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does this policy align with our broader economic goals?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do the economic benefits of this policy, such as potential tax revenues and investment funds, outweigh the incentives provided to foreigners to grow their retirement accounts in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These questions reflect the concerns and curiosity of some Singaporeans who may perceive the policy as the Government simply facilitating the growth of retirement funds for foreigners.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government share more about the policy considerations on this matter?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will individuals in the process of applying for SC/PR status be allowed to retain their CPF accounts during this period or are they required to close their accounts and later re-establish them upon attaining SC/PR status?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, I have queries on the policy amendments on the disclosure of deceased members' CPF information.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, how does the Board determine that such information will be accessed by individuals whom the deceased member did not intend to be beneficiaries?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The CPF system was set up as a compulsory savings plan for working Singaporeans and PRs primarily to fund their retirement, healthcare, education and housing needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should ensure that the system remains focused on its target beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, we should strive for efficiency and resident-centric administration of CPF schemes for better service delivery.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would CPF consider to stop paying any interest at all?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will CPF Board return the funds to account holders whose bank accounts are closed?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin): What is the deadline for the withdrawal of the monies?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the event of the death of account holders, what is the deadline for the family members or beneficiaries to claim the monies?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What happens if the account holder does not have any beneficiary in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What will CPF do with the unclaimed amount?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the money, for example, be included as part of the Ministry of Manpower's budget and be used for purposes, such as helping SMEs to train and develop their Singaporean workers?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If both the account holder and the spouse had passed on and the account owner had few children, will all their children be classified as the next-of-kin and receive the same amounts?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can he still get the deceased's CPF information?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked whether there are new considerations that led to these changes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, the amendments in this Bill are the final steps to ensure that the CPF system is focused on the core objective of supporting the retirement, housing and healthcare needs of residents here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked whether ceasing the participation of foreign workers in the CPF system will cause businesses and employers to turn away from Singaporeans since employers do not have to pay additional CPF contributions for foreign workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai is similarly concerned about Singaporean workers being less competitive than foreign workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Qualifying Salaries are benchmarked against local wages, inclusive of employer CPF contributions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The EP and S Pass Qualifying Salaries are benchmarked to the top one-third of local professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) and associate professionals and technicians (APTs) respectively.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Based on the way that we benchmark the wages of EP and S Pass holders, there is no wage-cost advantage for employers to hire foreign professionals.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is one area that Mr Leong has raised that I would like to dispel.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And this has been previously addressed in various Parliamentary Questions (PQs).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Leong's characterisation of EP salaries being lower than local PMETs is also inaccurate as we have been raising it regularly and have now benchmarked it to the top one-third of local PMET wages.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In fact, the $5,000 qualifying salary that Mr Leong cited is for a young EP – a young EP holder at the age of 23, just joining the workforce.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This increases progressively with age to $10,500 a month at age 45 and above.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And for the financial services sector, it is even higher, to take into account the consideration that there are higher salary norms in these other sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The rest of Mr Leong's obtuse and illogical argument to link this to CPF returns is outside the scope of this Bill and it is quite irrelevant to this discussion.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I will not attempt to do mental gymnastics with Members here in this House.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked how many non-resident accounts will be affected and whether we are going to do anything to prepare for the expected outflow of monies from the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Non-resident CPF balance is, in fact, only about 1% of all CPF balances.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the outflow of non-resident CPF balances will not pose liquidity issues.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Don Wee asked how much operational savings are expected as a result of these amendments.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To give Members some sense of the additional operational load on CPF Board to serve non-residents, let me explain that CPF Board has separate manual processes to manage service requests from non-residents, such as undertaking additional steps to verify their identity, as these non-residents do not have access to Singpass.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, ceasing the participation of non-residents in CPF will result in more efficiency for CPF Board.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked why the timeline to cease non-residents' participation in CPF schemes may differ for different groups of members.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There are broadly two different groups of members.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The first are existing non-residents who have already left Singapore or have not been working for some time here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The second are members who become non-residents after 1 April 2024.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For existing non-residents who are already known to us, we are able to process the accounts ahead of time so that their participation in CPF schemes will cease starting from 1 April 2024.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, for current residents who become non-residents only after 1 April 2024, we can only cease their participation in CPF schemes from the date that they renounce their Singapore Citizenship or their Permanent Residency.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, some time is required to wind up their participation in CPF schemes, depending on the specific circumstances.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether those in the process of applying for Singapore Citizenship or Permanent Residency can be allowed to continue participating in CPF schemes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Those who already hold Permanent Residency and are applying for Singapore Citizenship will continue to participate in CPF schemes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For non-residents who are applying for Permanent Residency, the general application processing time is about six months and some applications may take longer to process.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, for those who still hold non-resident status as of 1 April 2024, their participation in CPF schemes will cease.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Nonetheless, once they are granted Permanent Residency, they will then be part of the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CPF Board had also announced in March this year how non-residents' participation in CPF schemes will cease, which should give ample lead time for the transition of these members.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Don Wee also asked how CPF Board will return the CPF balances to account holders whose bank accounts are closed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Non-residents can choose to transfer their CPF monies to their local or overseas bank accounts or via cheques.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Don Wee also asked about the deadline for the transfer of monies by the member, or, if they are deceased, by their beneficiaries who may not be in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And while I would like to have additional budget for MOM's needs, we cannot use this money as part of MOM's operating budget or, for that matter, for any other purposes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if new citizens and PRs will have sufficient savings to be self-reliant.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In general, new citizens and PRs are required to either be economically active or have the means to support themselves through employment or family support.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CPF savings are not their only means to attain retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And, in fact, many Singaporeans and PRs also tap on their savings and family support to meet their own retirement needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether there are projections regarding the number of non-residents expected to sign up for the Supplementary Retirement Scheme, also known as SRS, and whether the Government is, in fact, facilitating the growth of retirement funds of non-residents by providing them tax relief through SRS.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SRS is operated by the private sector, where participation is voluntary and contributions are made through cash, not CPF monies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Contributions to SRS are separate from the CPF scheme and SRS is a mechanism for anyone who wishes to save money for retirement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, SRS members are able to use savings in their SRS account to invest in commercial investment products in the market and the investment returns from these commercial products can complement CPF to support their retirement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But it is, in fact, quite a separate thing from CPF.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The only thing they have in common, is that they help to add to the retirement adequacy needs of the individual.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, as SRS is voluntary, we are not able to predict the number of sign-ups.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Leong Mun Wai asked about whether the interest rates and returns of CPF accounts will increase in the future.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is not relevant to today's CPF (Amendment) Bill, but nonetheless, let me respond briefly by saying that the Ordinary, Special and MediSave Account interest rates are reviewed quarterly while the Retirement Account interest rate is reviewed annually, according to the pegged rates.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: When the pegged rates exceed the floor rates, members will correspondingly earn the higher interest rates on their CPF savings.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, we will continue to review the CPF interest rates to ensure that returns remain relevant while taking into consideration the longer-term outlook.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On aligning disclosure practices upon a member's death to industry practices, Members have asked questions about who will receive the deceased member's CPF information and what information will be disclosed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some Members have also asked questions on the disbursement of CPF monies after a member's death.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On who will receive the deceased member's CPF information, Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether the disclosure of deceased member's information is limited to one person or all of the next-of-kin, beneficiaries and nominees.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Don Wee also asked whether the information would be disclosed to a next-of-kin who is neither a nominee nor a beneficiary under the relevant intestacy laws.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: All nominees and the deceased's beneficiaries under the relevant intestacy laws will be allowed to access the deceased member's CPF information.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To be clear, if a family relation is not considered a next-of-kin under the relevant intestacy laws, they will not be allowed access to the deceased member's CPF information.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked what percentage of CPF members gave consent to CPF Board to disclose information after death when making their nominations of the persons entitled to receive their CPF monies upon their death.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked whether the amendments entail information being accessed by those not intended by the deceased member.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Today, nine in 10 members who make nominations have already authorised all their nominees to access their CPF information upon the members' demise.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, for the vast majority of those members today, the amendments are, in fact, aligned with their intentions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Being able to access the deceased member's CPF information and nomination details without requiring explicit authorisation by deceased members is aligned to industry practice for wills and intestate distribution of assets by the Public Trustee.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is intended to provide convenience to settle deceased member's post-demise matters.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It also ensures transparency so that all nominees and beneficiaries under the relevant intestacy laws are assured that the deceased members' CPF monies have been fully accounted for.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On what information will be disclosed, Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked whether the information that nominees and beneficiaries under the relevant intestacy laws can access is broader in scope than what authorised members can access today.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In general, only details that will help nominees or beneficiaries under relevant intestacy laws settle the deceased member's post-demise matters will be disclosed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will include details of the deceased's participation in CPF schemes, but exclude details of the relationships between nominee and the deceased, as well as information on the deceased's witnesses to the nomination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the disbursement of CPF monies after a member's death, Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked what percentage of deceased members' CPF monies was not disbursed within a month and remained unclaimed six months after the notification of death to CPF Board.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, if there is a valid nomination, it will go to the surviving nominees, which may or may not be the children, depending on the nomination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On allowing transactions to continue after a member's death, Mr Louis Ng asked what practical effect these amendments will have for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As explained in my opening speech, the amendments seek to clarify the Board's powers to process the necessary transactions after a member's date of death.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Singaporeans will not experience any changes in the computation of the CPF balances to be paid out to the nominees and beneficiaries under the relevant intestacy laws.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Bill will allow us to continue to focus the CPF system on supporting residents' retirement, housing and healthcare needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Residents will also benefit from the streamlined administration of CPF schemes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do Members have any clarifications for the Senior Minister of State?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have discussed or debated about this several times with the Minister and also the Senior Minister of State, over the course of the last few years in this House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And the reasons that the Minister and the Senior Minister of State have given, are the same as what he had said today – that that disadvantage for the Singaporean workers has been mitigated through adjusting the minimum Qualifying Salary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But what I would like to clarify and like to say is that one, there are two things about the minimum Qualifying Salary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is that the Minister and the Senior Minister of State has said that the minimum Qualifying Salary will be adjusted according to the age of the EP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But that adjustment is not totally transparent to the public or to all of us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We need more information as to how they adjust that and then that would negate the negative impact on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, I think I would also like to point out that it is only in recent years that a minimum Qualifying Salary has been adjusted upwards many times.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For the longest time, since 2000, when we opened the flood gates for foreign workers, the minimum Qualifying Salaries has actually remained at very low levels.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I would like the Senior Minister of State to explain how adjusting the minimum Qualifying Salaries can totally negate the negative impact of Singaporeans workers having to pay CPF but EPs do not have to pay CPF.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any clarifications to seek from Senior Minister of State Koh?
